title: Five Nepali ministers attend COP31 in Turkey, raising questions over size of delegation - OnlineKhabar English News
description: Five Nepali ministers attend COP31 in Turkey, raising questions over size of delegation  OnlineKhabar English News
publisher.title: OnlineKhabar English News
full_article:
Kathmandu, November 13

Five Nepali ministers have travelled to Antalya, Turkey, to attend the 31st United Nations Climate Change Conference (COP31), prompting questions over whether all of them needed to be present at the international gathering.

The conference, which has been underway for five days, has brought together government representatives and experts from around the world. Nepal has sent Foreign Minister Shishir Khanal and Minister for Agriculture, Forests and Environment Geeta Chaudhary as its official political representatives, while three other ministers have also attended various sessions and side events.

Foreign Minister Khanal is scheduled to return to Nepal on Saturday. Chaudhary will represent the country in the sessions that follow.

Education Minister Sasmit Pokharel left for Turkey on Friday to participate in COP-related programmes. Finance Minister Dr Swarnim Wagle is already attending the conference, while Health Minister Nisha Mehta visited the conference venue before travelling to Sri Lanka for a programme. She returned to Nepal on Thursday.

According to a statement issued by the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, Nepal’s official delegation includes Khanal, Chaudhary, National Planning Commission member Professor Dr Sanjay Acharya, Agriculture, Forests and Environment Ministry Secretary Dr Rajendra Prasad Mishra and other senior government officials.

The other ministers, lawmakers and officials who travelled to the conference outside the formal delegation have arranged their participation in different programmes.

Initially, only Environment Minister Chaudhary was scheduled to attend COP31. However, Prime Minister Balendra Shah wanted Foreign Minister Khanal to lead the delegation, after which the government decided to send both ministers as official representatives.

Khanal addressed the conference’s opening session. He also spoke at a programme jointly organised by Nepal, Tajikistan, Kyrgyzstan, Bhutan and Pakistan.

Nepal has established a pavilion at the conference venue, where discussions on climate change and related issues are being held through various sessions. Other Nepali ministers attending the conference have also participated as speakers at the pavilion.

Nepal had sought to include Himalayan issues in the conference’s formal agenda, a proposal also supported by Bhutan. However, the issue was not included, with developed countries giving it limited attention, according to the report.

Khanal raised the issue again at a programme on Friday, calling for grant-based, predictable and concessional climate finance to address the needs of countries vulnerable to climate change.

Speaking at a high-level event on climate finance needs and access for small island developing states and least developed countries, Khanal called for easier and direct access to climate funding.

He said countries such as Nepal, which have contributed negligibly to climate change, should not be forced to take on additional debt in the name of climate resilience.

“Climate resilience must not come at the cost of debt sustainability. We need predictable public grants and highly concessional financial resources, not commercial loans,” he said.

Finance Minister Wagle, who travelled to Antalya on Monday, is scheduled to represent Nepal and advocate for the country’s positions on climate change and sustainable economic development at around half a dozen high-level sessions, according to his secretariat.

On November 10, he addressed a programme on the Systematic Observations Financing Facility at the UNFCCC Pavilion.

Health Minister Mehta chaired a panel discussion at the Nepal Pavilion, where she called for climate change to be recognised as a serious public health crisis and for health to be placed at the centre of climate action plans.

After the discussion, she travelled to Colombo, Sri Lanka, to attend the first BIMSTEC Health Ministers’ Meeting.

Environment Minister Chaudhary has raised issues including the protection of Himalayan ecosystems, easier access to adaptation finance, compensation for loss and damage, and climate action led by local communities.

Speaking at a Nepal Pavilion session on the ‘Living Sagarmatha: Nepal Himalayan Resilience Strategy’, Chaudhary said the strategy brings together fragmented programmes in the Himalayan region under a unified national approach covering biodiversity, sustainable forest management and the health of the cryosphere.

She said 35 priority areas had been identified to protect rural livelihoods through Himalayan agriculture, herbal production and the development of value chains for local products. Implementing these priorities would require investment of more than USD 4 billion, she said.

Chaudhary also described the protection of the Himalayas as a shared global responsibility, noting that the region is linked to the water and climate security of nearly two billion people.

Referring to climate-related disasters in the Himalayan region, including floods in Rasuwa, she highlighted their direct effects on public health and service delivery and called for easier access to grant-based climate finance for least developed countries.

The participation of large numbers of government officials in international climate conferences has drawn criticism in previous years, with concerns that such events are sometimes treated as opportunities for travel rather than substantive engagement.

Questions have also emerged this year over whether all five ministers needed to attend the conference.

Former minister Dr Madan Pariyar, who attended COP30 last year, said the substance of a country’s participation mattered more than the size of its delegation.

“What matters is not how many people attend, but what agenda they present and how they present it,” he said, adding that COP conferences also include numerous side events beyond the main sessions.

Environmentalist Bhushan Tuladhar said COP31 was important for Nepal, but the roles played by individual ministers should be examined to assess their participation.

“As far as I know, the foreign, finance and environment ministers appear to have had clear reasons to attend. In the case of the other ministers, their programmes need to be examined before drawing conclusions,” Tuladhar said.

title: Nepal wants climate funding for disaster preparedness, not just recovery, says UN coordinator - ThePrint
description: Nepal wants climate funding for disaster preparedness, not just recovery, says UN coordinator  ThePrint
publisher.title: ThePrint
full_article:
“Nepal understands that climate resilience is an investment, not an expense—proactive prevention, data-backed financial collateral, and risk-informed infrastructure cost far less than repeated destruction and post-disaster recovery,” she said, responding to ThePrint’s questions from Türkiye’s Antalya.

On 26 August this year, Nepal was hit by devastating flash floods, sweeping away houses, bridges, roads and leaving at least 1,500 people dead and hundreds missing or displaced. The sudden surge of water, triggered by an ice-and-rock collapse and subsequent outburst near the Nepal-Tibet border, inundated settlements along the Bhote Koshi river basin.

At Antalya, the Nepal delegation has asked for a dedicated mountain agenda, along with Bhutan and mountain allies, to formally recognise and give dedicated focus to mountain ecosystems. The country delegation has also brought the world’s attention to securing direct, simplified access to recovery and reconstruction funds that reflect the true scale of post-disaster needs without burdening climate-vulnerable nations with unsustainable debt. It also stresses transboundary data and regional cooperation, among other pressing climate action.

The Rasuwa flash floods

Yahia said that the Rasuwa floods were not an isolated event—the same river flooded just a year ago, and in October the Budhigandaki flooded in Gorkha. Rapid warming across high-altitude mountain regions, she said, was posing a severe risk to glaciers, water security, and rural livelihoods, erasing years of hard-won development progress in hours.

“For survivors—especially women who have lost spouses—lost homes and livelihoods, it is dealing with compounding debt and long-term socio-economic vulnerability,” she said.

Yahia added that targeted adaptation and localised response efforts are proving effective.

“Nepal’s early warning systems demonstrated their critical value when a second flood struck six weeks after the Rasuwa flood, successfully alerting communities and saving lives,” she said.

Yahia explained that the country maintains a highly experienced, trained search and rescue team accustomed to navigating extreme mountain terrain.

Driven by hard-learned lessons from past disasters, she said, Nepal is actively modernising its immediate disaster response, operational logistics, and institutional capacities.

“For example, Nepal is shifting from reactive disaster aid to proactive risk financing. It is deploying cargo drones for rapid emergency deliveries across impassable terrain, digitalising social protection and emergency cash transfers, and streamlining supply distribution channels,” Yahia said.

She added that Nepal is also leveraging operational data from these recurring shocks to advocate for direct access to international Loss and Damage funds. She said it would help to “bridge the widening gap between immediate post-disaster recovery costs and national development budgets.”

Adaptation

Yahia stressed that for Nepal, adaptation means breaking the cycle of rebuilding the same vulnerabilities after every disaster.

Through the government-led, UN-supported Living Sagarmatha Strategy—a $4.08 billion, 10-year investment roadmap—Nepal is establishing a unified framework to protect its high-altitude ecosystems, secure vital water systems, and build a climate-resilient economy.

She said that because Himalayan glaciers supply the headwaters for over 1.3 billion people downstream, Nepal treats mountain adaptation not merely as a national priority, but as a regional and global public good.

“Nepal understands that climate resilience is an investment, not an expense—proactive prevention, data-backed financial collateral, and risk-informed infrastructure cost far less than repeated destruction and post-disaster recovery,” she said.

Under the Sagarmatha vision, adaptation is anchored in forward-looking infrastructure, cutting-edge technology, and innovative financing.

For example, Nepal is investing in a nationwide systemic climate and cryosphere observatory—integrating satellite imagery, AI analytics, seismic/hydrological sensors, and high-altitude monitoring stations.

The granular, continuous risk and environmental data generated by these observatories serves as financial collateral: verifiable baseline data lowers risk premiums, unlocks parametric insurance, attracts global private climate investment, and validates resilience returns for international climate finance.

“It involves adopting a national Early Warnings for All roadmap and fostering cross-border collaboration to manage shared transboundary river-basin and climate risks; re-engineering how shelter, roads, bridges, and hydropower projects are planned and built—integrating multi-hazard climate assessments so critical national assets and local housing withstand extreme weather events,” Yahia said.

Climate finance for vulnerable nations

The provisionally set aside $21.6 million for Nepal from the UN Fund for Responding to Loss and Damage is a very positive step, marking the first time the fund has responded to a specific disaster, the UN resident coordinator said.

But she added that it covers less than 0.5 per cent of the country’s recovery needs.

“Nepal’s preliminary Post-Disaster Needs Assessment estimates total recovery and reconstruction costs at approximately USD 4.7 billion—for a country that contributes just ~0.1% of global greenhouse emissions. Clearly, traditional international aid and national fiscal budgets alone cannot fill this gap,” she said.

According to the coordinator, to achieve true long-term resilience without taking on unsustainable debt, climate finance for vulnerable nations like Nepal must evolve from reactive post-disaster handouts into a diversified combination of grants, highly concessional finance, and innovative disaster risk financing.

The roadmap to scaling up climate finance to 1.3 trillion annually provides vital pathways; there is a clear need to see faster progress moving it closer to reality, she added.

Also read: COP31 president calls for action as climate meet opens in Turkey

Nepal at COP31

Yahia said that the government of Nepal has spoken strongly about what is needed, particularly clear progress that helps to ensure humanity can keep the overshoot of the 1.5 degree global heating limit as short and shallow as possible. “Nepal has also been very clear about the need to recognise the unique vulnerabilities of mountain regions, and scale up accessible, highly concessional, and non-debt-creating climate finance,” Yahia said.

Above all, she said, Nepal seeks special acknowledgement by the international community of the horrific human and economic toll of recent climate disasters—such as the catastrophic Rasuwa and Budhigandaki floods. Nepal is asking the global community for explicit solidarity, translated into dedicated, predictable financial mechanisms for long-term recovery, reconstruction, and Loss and Damage.

(Edited by Ratan Priya)

title: Nepal and South Korea Sign Climate Change Cooperation Framework Agreement - Ratopati
description: Nepal and South Korea Sign Climate Change Cooperation Framework Agreement  Ratopati
publisher.title: Ratopati
full_article:
Turkie. Nepal and the Republic of Korea (South Korea) have signed a framework agreement on cooperation on climate change with the objective of reducing climate change, mobilizing carbon finance, and reducing greenhouse gas emissions.

The agreement, reached under Article 6 of the Paris Agreement, is expected to create new opportunities for cooperation between the two countries in the areas of carbon markets, climate-friendly investment, technology transfer, climate adaptation, and sustainable development.

Under the agreement, emission reduction projects can be developed between Nepal and South Korea, and internationally recognized emission reduction achievements can be transferred. It is believed that this will mobilize international carbon finance and promote public and private sector investment in climate adaptation and mitigation.

The agreement covers renewable energy, transport, industry, buildings, waste management, agriculture, and forestry as priority areas for cooperation. Climate-friendly project development, investment expansion, and the use of modern technology will be encouraged in these areas.

Similarly, the agreement includes a transparent accounting, monitoring, reporting, and verification (MRV) system for carbon emissions, an adjustment process, and a mechanism to prevent double counting of emission reductions. This will help maintain environmental integrity in carbon trading and fulfill international climate commitments.

In addition to carbon markets, the two countries will also cooperate in the fields of climate science, research, technological innovation, climate adaptation, methane emission reduction, and just energy transition. The agreement states that knowledge, skills, and technology will be exchanged between government agencies, universities, researchers, investors, and private sector organizations for this purpose.

This agreement is also expected to be important for the implementation of Nepal's Nationally Determined Contribution (NDC) 3.0, enhancing climate resilience, and achieving the goal of net-zero greenhouse gas emissions by 2045.

A joint committee on climate change cooperation, comprising government representatives from both countries, will be formed to implement the agreement, approve joint work plans, and monitor cooperation activities. The committee can also form special sub-committees on carbon market mechanisms and climate science and technology as needed.

At a time when Nepal is facing serious challenges due to climate change, including floods, landslides, and increasing risks in the Himalayan region, the Government of Nepal has expressed confidence that such international partnerships will contribute to mobilizing climate finance, developing technology, and enhancing national capacity.

Nepal expects to transform the opportunities gained from the agreement into concrete investment, technology partnerships, capacity development, and measurable climate achievements.

Previously, Nepal signed an Emission Reduction Payment Agreement (ERPA) with LEAF Coalition under the REDD+ program last year. The South Korean government is also a partner in this program.

The agreement was signed by Dr. Maheshwar Dhakal, Joint Secretary and Focal Point for the UNFCCC on behalf of the Government of Nepal, and Jongho Kyun, Ambassador for Climate Change and Deputy Minister of Foreign Affairs on behalf of the Government of South Korea.

The Government of Nepal has expressed gratitude to the Government of South Korea for the partnership and commitment, and expressed confidence that this agreement will further expand effective, transparent, and mutually beneficial climate cooperation between the two countries.

full_article:
Kathmandu. Today is Friday, Kartik 27, 2083 BS. We are here with the main events of the day with Ratopati's night presentation 'Ratopati Briefing' - '10 o'clock 10' news.

1. Victims Still Suffering

Eighty days have passed since the devastating flood in the Bhotekoshi River on Bhadra 10, but the victims have not yet received government relief and rehabilitation. The flood damaged about 7,500 houses in Rasuwa, Nuwakot, Dhading, and Gorkha, leaving thousands of citizens homeless. More than 5,200 people were reported missing in the disaster. The daily lives of the displaced, who barely managed to save their lives, are becoming increasingly difficult.

80 days have passed since the Bhotekoshi flood, but instead of relief, the government has provided suffering

2. Weather Information

As the influence of the westerly wind gradually increases, there is a possibility of rain and snowfall starting in the hilly and Himalayan regions of Sudurpashchim, Karnali, and Gandaki provinces from Sunday. Meteorologists have advised farmers to secure the remaining paddy crops in the fields and the straw being dried, as some places may experience thunderstorms, lightning, and hail. According to Vibhuti Pokharel, a meteorologist at the Department of Hydrology and Meteorology, the weather across the country will be generally clear on Friday and Saturday. Although there will be light rain in scattered places in the hilly and mountainous regions on these two days, there will be no major weather changes. From Sunday, the westerly wind will become active, and the weather will change from the high-altitude areas of Sudurpashchim and Karnali, with the possibility of its influence extending to Gandaki province. It is also estimated that there may be sporadic rainfall in a few places in the hilly regions of Bagmati and Koshi provinces.

Is there rice in the fields? Meteorologists urge to bring it in before Sunday

3. Public Holiday

The government has declared Monday (Kartik 30) a public holiday. Anand Kafle, spokesperson for the Ministry of Home Affairs, issued a notice on Friday informing about the public holiday. A total of 19 public holidays have fallen in the month of Kartik alone in the current fiscal year 2083 BS. Including various festivals and additional holidays declared by the government, the number of public holidays in Kartik has reached 19. The number of public holidays has increased after the government decided to give an additional public holiday on Monday, Kartik 30. The high number of public holidays is due to major festivals like Dashain and Tihar falling in this month.

The government declared Monday a public holiday

19 days of public holidays in the month of Kartik alone

4. Judicial Appointments

President Ram Chandra Paudel has appointed four judges to the Supreme Court. The newly appointed judges were administered the oath of office and secrecy by Chief Justice Dr. Manoj Sharma on Friday in the presence of President Paudel. The judges also took office today.

4 Supreme Court judges take oath

Four newly appointed judges take office

5. Uncontrolled EV Speed on Roads

On Thursday morning, around 5:45 AM, an electric (EV) microbus traveling from Kathmandu to Sarlahi met with an accident on the Bhimfedi-Kulekhani-Kathmandu road section in Makwanpur, on the Chisapani descent, resulting in 14 deaths and 6 serious injuries. The accident, which occurred while the vehicle was carrying passengers returning home to celebrate the Chhath festival, has sparked a serious debate in Nepal about the safety standards of electric vehicles, road and charging infrastructure, specialized driver training, and the lack of government regulation.

No standards, no infrastructure: Uncontrolled EV speed on the roads

6. Strictness After Accident

The Kathmandu District Administration Office has set a new time limit for the operation of passenger and public vehicles plying the Balkhu-Dakshinkali route to Hetauda. As per the decision of the District Security Committee Kathmandu, passenger vehicles operating on this route must now reach the police check post in Pharping by 8 PM. Similarly, vehicles will only be allowed to operate on this route from Balkhu starting at 5 AM.

Time limit for vehicles going to Hetauda via Balkhu-Dakshinkali, can only operate from 5 AM

7. Ambassador Follow-up

Of the 10 ambassadors to various countries approved by the Parliamentary Hearing Committee, agréments have been received for ambassadors to three countries. According to sources from the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, agréments have been received from the respective countries for the ambassadors to India, China, and Israel.

The ambassadors of three countries have reached an agreement

8. Congress Statute

The working committee led by Gagan Thapa, elected from the 15th General Convention of the Nepali Congress, and the Statute Election Commission have not yet updated the statute. The 15th General Convention, held in Kathmandu from Ashoj 18 to 23, amended the Congress's statute and increased the number of working committee members and office bearers. A new working committee was formed through elections based on that amended statute.

Congress's new working committee and statute not yet updated

9. Police

With the removal of Dan Bahadur Karki from the post of Inspector General (IGP) of Nepal Police, one AIG post has become vacant in the police force. Karki was appointed to a newly created position of 'Special Security Advisor to the Prime Minister' by the Council of Ministers. This position created for Karki remains in the Prime Minister's Office and Council of Ministers.

One AIG post is vacant in the police, two DIG posts are becoming vacant

10. Share Market

The stock market saw a slight decline on Friday. The market, which opened after a week due to the Tihar holidays, closed down by 6.48 points at 2648.74 points. Today, among the companies that traded, the share price of 160 companies decreased, while the share price of 109 companies increased. The share price of 10 companies remained stable.

title: Hicksville brothers hope changing brand of Glen Cove Nepali eatery boosts business - Newsday
description: Hicksville brothers hope changing brand of Glen Cove Nepali eatery boosts business  Newsday
publisher.title: Newsday
full_article:
As brothers Bikash and Parash Kharel worked to introduce Glen Cove to Nepali cuisine, a customer base largely unfamiliar with the food, along with rising tariffs, left them in a difficult position just two years after opening their restaurant.

They had brought While in Kathmandu, renamed Delhi to Kathmandu in August, to Glen Cove in 2024 after years of success at the original location in Ridgewood, Queens.

When the eatery opened on Glen Street, Bikash Kharel, 32, of Hicksville, said he envisioned that at least a third of its clientele would be young adults and college students. But they didn't show up in the numbers he had anticipated.

Parash Kharel, 37, also of Hicksville, said he and his brother, both born in Nepal, fell in love with Glen Cove on childhood fishing trips and had hoped to re-create the lively atmosphere of the Ridgewood establishment, where twentysomethings often fill the bar seats.

"In the initial phases, we definitely saw good local reception ... but we experienced that it was an older eating group ... and their palate, with our food, was not the best match," said Bikash Kharel, referencing both the spiciness of their dishes and an unfamiliarity with Nepali cuisine as the reasons.

Tariffs take a toll

President Donald Trump's new tariffs on imported products in 2025 exacerbated the issue.

Month after month, tariffs on key ingredients imported from Nepal, like fermented leafy greens called gundruk, and low foot traffic at the restaurant started to weigh on them. After labor and operating costs, Parash Kharel said, the eatery was barely profitable.

He began to ask himself if the restaurant was worth the sacrifice.

But their father, Bed P. Kharel, pushed the brothers. After immigrating to the United States from Nepal in 2001, the elder Kharel worked at an Indian restaurant. Bikash Kharel said this was common among Nepali immigrants at the time.

Parash Kharel at Delhi To Kathmandu, in Glen Cove, on Monday. Credit: Newsday/Alejandra Villa Loarca

Eventually, their father opened his own Indian restaurants, one in Ridgewood on the same street where Bikash Kharel would open While in Kathmandu, with his brother soon joining him.

"The thing about being a small-business owner, you can never give up. I mean, that's something our daddy instilled in us. ... If something doesn't work out, try another way," Parash Kharel said.

So he leaned into adjusting to the Glen Cove market, bringing live jazz on Friday nights and decreasing the spice level of the food based on each customer’s preference.

Bestsellers after rebranding

In August, the duo rebranded the entire spot to an Indian-Nepali fusion restaurant with a new menu and name. One bestseller has been a Nepali staple called momos, which are dumplings, with an option to add Indian butter sauce — an American favorite often paired with chicken.

"Water buffalo momo is something that is more than comfort to us. When we're kids, especially my generation, we used to get a couple of bucks to go to lunch. You could get a water buffalo momo with jhol," Parash Kharel explained. Jhol is a savory soup. "Every day I'm pretty much retelling the whole story again and again."

The business issues weren’t unique to the Kharel brothers' establishment.

Before Delhi to Kathmandu, the space had been occupied by an Indian restaurant called Tava, which opened in 2021 and closed in 2024. Right next door at 63 Glen St., Parash has seen three restaurants come and go: a Thai restaurant named Thaiana, a fast-casual Asian eatery called Coo Coo Kitchen and most recently a Hawaiian restaurant called Lulu Hawaii.

Even at the Ridgewood location, things are changing.

When Bikash Kharel opened While in Kathmandu in 2017, he said, Ridgewood was in the early stages of gentrification, which was initially great for business. But as the neighborhood continued to evolve, he began to worry about the restaurant becoming a "has-been."

It's leaning into Ridgewood’s new fine dining landscape with dishes like lamb chop braised with chhyang, which is a sweet, tangy, mildly alcoholic fermented grain. The entree is served with tomatoes and a wild perilla seed called silam on traditional bronze plates called chares.

"We’re using primarily Nepali ingredients to showcase a dish that is already readily popular in the American marketplace ... using both sides of where I come from and where I am," Bikash Kharel said. The new Ridgewood menu debuts later this month.

Parash Kharel said he has seen more foot traffic after changing the menu but still has concerns.

"We're doing good, but then again doing good business and being profitable is another thing ... just making enough to pay the bills," he said.

Realistically, it would help to raise prices. While customers were understanding of that decision in Ridgewood, Parash Kharel added, it would be less welcome in Glen Cove. With a faltering economy, he said, even regulars who used to frequent the restaurant several times a month told him they can’t afford to come in as often anymore.

"We are looking for a solution, but we're also hoping it'll pass," he said. "It's not only me, as a small business, hurting. I think it's the everyday people. Everyday folks are hurting, too."

Newsday's Erica Marcus contributed to this story.

title: Over Forty Percent of Parsa Health Volunteers Experience Depression in Nepal - Bioengineer.org
description: Over Forty Percent of Parsa Health Volunteers Experience Depression in Nepal  Bioengineer.org
publisher.title: Bioengineer.org
full_article:
A cross-sectional study published in BMC Public Health found that 41.3 percent of female community health volunteers in Nepal’s Parsa district experienced depression, while 19.8 percent experienced anxiety. Conducted by researchers Navin Yadav and Tulsi Ram Bhandari, the investigation assessed psychological morbidity and social determinants across all 14 local administrative levels of the district to evaluate mental health conditions among peripheral health workers.

Female community health volunteers represent a vital pillar of Nepal’s healthcare system, operating as local women who deliver essential care from the periphery of their communities. The Government of Nepal has recognized their instrumental contributions to achieving Millennium Development Goals 4 and 5, and national health strategies anticipate a similar foundational role through contextual adaptation during the Sustainable Development Goals framework extending to 2030.

To assess psychological outcomes, the researchers implemented a cross-sectional study design utilizing probability proportionate sampling across all 14 local levels in Parsa. Trained personnel collected primary data through face-to-face interviews using a standardized interview schedule, subsequently entering the records into EpiData version 3.1 before transferring the dataset to the Statistical Package for the Social Sciences version 20 for statistical evaluation.

Multivariable logistic regression revealed that participant religion, family type, and the educational status of the respondent’s husband were significantly associated with both depression and anxiety at a threshold of p < 0.05.

Conversely, volunteers residing in joint families exhibited lower odds of anxiety than those living in nuclear family arrangements, recording an odds ratio of 0.29 and a 95 percent confidence interval of 0.10 to 0.86. Kathmandu, Nov 13: Outgoing President of the Federation of Nepalese Chambers of Commerce and Industry, Chandra Prasad Dhakal, urged the investors of United Arab Emirates to invest in Nepal's hydropower, tourism, agriculture, information technology and data centre.

President Dhakal, who is in UAE to participate in RAK Investment Summit' organised at Ras Al Khaimah of UAE, made this request during the meeting with Minister or Foreign Trade UAE, Dr Thani bin Ahmed Al Zeyoudi, on Thursday.

On the occasion, they discussed the Nepal-UAE relations, trade expansion and opportunity of available investment in Nepal, according to Dhakal's Private Secretariat.

Appreciating the operation of direct flight from UAE to Pokhara International Airport, Dhakal requested to take initiatives for the operation of direct flight to Bhairahawa-based Gautam Buddha International Airport. (RSS)

KATHMANDU, Nov 13 : India's newly appointed ambassador to Nepal Sudhakar Dalela on Thursday met the Himalayan nation's foreign secretary Amrit Bahadur Rai and discussed ways to further strengthen bilateral ties.

The meeting at the foreign ministry took place ahead of Nepal Prime Minister Balendra Shah's proposed visit to India later in the month.

"They held productive discussions on various facets of bilateral cooperation and ways to further strengthen close ties of friendship and cooperation," the Indian embassy in Kathmandu said in a post on X.
